title: Assessing Schools
author: Matthew Evans
summary: Evans, who still carries scars from an Ofsted inspection, argues that school inspection remains a legitimate part of accountability but is badly overloaded. He says the key disagreement is whether a short visit can deliver a definitive holistic judgement of a school, and he proposes instead treating inspection as one tool among several. Using assessment theory, he separates inference validity from consequential validity and applies them to four things inspectors judge: compliance, provision, cultural norms and processes. Visits suit cultural norms but not compliance or provision, and for processes with uncertain causal links, such as teaching and leadership, inspectors lean on weak proxies like exam outcomes. He proposes more frequent compliance audits, better data on provision, long-term inspector relationships, assessment across trusts, and a dashboard drawing on multiple sources to reduce the unfairness that breaks careers.
points: Inspection should be judged as part of the wider accountability ecosystem, not as the pinnacle of it.
Different school constructs need different assessment methods: visits fit culture, while compliance and provision can be checked more often and without a visit.
Inferring teaching and leadership quality from exam outcomes means schools with weak intakes almost always receive poor judgements across the board.
What breaks school leaders is unfairness, when labels describe intake or when inferences lack validity, not accountability itself.
A dashboard built from multiple data sources would allow continuous improvement without the periodic overhaul of the inspection regime.
quotes: I support the idea of inspection firstly because it has helped improve standards of education in this country, secondly because school leaders should be accountable to the public, and thirdly because independent assessors should, now and again, visit schools to observe first hand what is going on.

There is an alternative view of the role inspection can play which is that it can provide useful information about some aspects of school standards alongside other indicators. Rather than inspection being the pinnacle of the accountability hierarchy, this view sees inspection as one tool among a range of measures.
From this perspective, school accountability is essentially an assessment problem because we are asking how best to assess (measure and make inferences about) educational standards.

Two-day inspections do a lot of heavy lifting which they are really not up to. Although an inspection process includes multiple forms of assessment, including talking to staff and students, examining data, and observing practice, the format only stretches so far.
In this way, a school with below average outcomes almost always ends up with a poor judgement on curriculum and teaching, and therefore on leadership.

We know that the current inspection system weighs heavily on schools and, at its worst, breaks people and careers. I know many headteachers who have been casualties of this system. None deny the importance of accountability. What breaks people is unfairness.
A simple dashboard which brings together the various data and judgements is all that is needed to provide parents and government with the information it needs to make informed decisions.
If any industry can design an intelligent accountability system, it should be ours. After all, assessment is our bread and butter.
